summary:
ARES is a web map that helps plan a safe human Marswalk across a specific patch of Mars. We focused on the boxwork area of Gale crater on Mount Sharp, where Curiosity has studied boxwork formations. The astronaut picks science stops, and ARES computes a walking route over real terrain that avoids slopes too steep for a person in a spacesuit. 

The map layers NASA data: a HiRISE digital terrain model (University of Arizona, NASA/JPL) is turned into slope and hillshade layers, Mars Trek provides the surface basemap, and Curiosity traverse waypoints supply the stop locations. For each route, ARES shows distance, estimated walking time, maximum slope and an elevation profile, and it explains why a route is not possible when no safe path exists.

Today astronauts would have to combine regional maps by hand. ARES brings the data needed for one excursion into a single view, with safety first. All assumptions and sources are shown in the app.
details:
What it does. ARES is a web map for planning one human Marswalk on a specific patch of Mars: the boxwork area of Gale crater on Mount Sharp. The user chooses a group of science stops, and the app computes a walking route from the start through each stop. The route avoids terrain steeper than 15 degrees, a limit we assume for a person in a spacesuit with equipment. For every route it shows distance, estimated walking time at 2km/h, maximum slope and an elevation profile. If no safe path exists, it says which leg fails and why.

How it works. We turned a HiRISE digital terrain model (DTEEC_009149_1750_009294_1750_U01, NASA/JPL/University of Arizona) into a 2 m elevation grid. Slope is computed over a smoothed window of about 5 m to reduce noise, and the same gradient drives a hillshade layer. A Python backend (FastAPI) runs an A* search over the slope grid. The map layers the slope and hillshade imagery over a Mars Trek basemap, and the stops come from Curiosity traverse waypoints.

Benefits and impact. Today the data an astronaut needs for one excursion is spread across regional and global tools. ARES puts terrain, safety limits and route in one view at the scale of a single outing. Every number comes from the NASA data and from assumptions listed in the app, so a crew or scientist can see where it came from and change it.

Tools. React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL, Python, FastAPI, NumPy, Vercel, GitHub. We used Claude Code (AI assistant) for parts of the development and AI-generated images on the landing page.

What is creative. Instead of another global Mars viewer, we built a hyperlocal tool around one decision: where can a person safely walk. The route comes from real terrain, and the map is designed as a planning screen a crew could use in a habitat or on a tablet.

What we considered. Safety first: slope limits drive the route, unsafe terrain is shown in red. We were honest about limits: routing uses slope only (no boulders, soil or radiation yet), the site bounday is preliminary, and the grid is 4 m. Future work: radiation and thermal layers, more sites, a return-to-habitat leg, and time and supply budgets.
